how-much-to-charge-to-install-an-automat.text:
← Automatic driveway gate bid calculator

How much to charge to install an automatic gate

A published $4,500 automatic-gate special treats a 12-foot single aluminum swing on existing posts as the same job as a 16-foot dual steel swing with masonry columns, two vehicle loops, a keypad, and a solar kit. It is not. Fence calculators price posts and walk gates as a barrier. Garage-door calculators price springs and a header. Automating the driveway is a style, an operator count, and the extra work you have to do before the leaves move. Quoting all of that from a kit special is how the first loop sawcut eats the field margin.

A job with the same opening can cost much more

Each extra operator is a kit that never appears on the brochure. On the sample rates a 12-foot single aluminum swing on existing posts with AC and two remotes prices about $6,506 ($542 per opening foot, 12.9 crew-hours, walk-away $4,684). The same shop’s 16-foot dual steel swing with masonry columns, two loops, a keypad, battery backup, edge sensors, and a solar kit prices about $20,440 ($1,277 per opening foot, 42.9 hours). Almost half of that dual bid is extra work — columns, loops, power, and access. Matching the single-swing special on the dual masonry gate is how that job becomes a loss. Even the cheap job’s walk-away ($4,684) is already above a $4,500 Facebook number.

Single swing looks cheaper until the posts are not there

Hanging two operators on posts that do not exist is a callback, not a savings. On a 16-foot steel opening the sample rates price a single swing with masonry around $15,395 — still thousands less than dual, because dual adds a second operator and a third column. Slide of that run prices about $16,741. Single swing is still the right bid on a 12-foot existing-post job: dual of that refresh prices about $9,165 and slide about $7,585 because you would be buying a second operator the opening does not need. Treating every driveway as one kit number is how the style that looked cheapest on paper is not the one that keeps the margin.

A slide with steel posts is not automatically the cheap 12-foot job

An 18-foot aluminum slide on new steel posts with one loop is not the 12-foot single plus 50%. On the sample rates that slide prices about $10,144 ($564 per opening foot, 22.8 crew-hours). The track and the receiver posts are their own hours. A 14-foot single wood swing on steel posts with a loop, keypad, and battery prices about $9,809 ($701 per opening foot). Neither number lives in a $4,500 kit special.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h hand loaded at 32% payroll burden is $55.44. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is arithmetic on the rates you type. It is not a gate specification, a UL 325 determination, a permit, an electrical design, an engineering stamp, or a recommendation of swing versus slide. Soil, slope, leaf weight versus operator class, and what the jurisdiction will accept still decide the style. Verify every figure against your own takeoff.

No warranty. This free page is not gate, construction, electrical, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. Open the bid calculator to price a specific opening.

Common questions

How much to charge to install an automatic gate?

Charge from the style (single swing, dual swing, or slide), the opening width, leaf material, columns, power, vehicle loops, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 12-foot single aluminum swing on existing posts at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $6,506 — about $542 per opening foot.

When is a dual swing more than a single-swing kit special?

When the opening needs two operators and the posts are not already there. On the sample rates a 16-foot dual steel swing with masonry columns, two loops, a keypad, and a solar kit prices around $20,440. Matching a $4,500 single-swing special on that job is how the first loop sawcut eats the field margin. Almost half of that dual bid is columns, loops, power, and access.

How much to charge for a sliding driveway gate?

A slide is one operator and a track, not a pair of swing leaves. On the sample rates an 18-foot aluminum slide on new steel posts with one loop prices around $10,144 ($564 per opening foot, 22.8 crew-hours). The track and the receiver posts do not live in a per-opening Facebook special.

        Common questions

        What does this gate estimate include?

        The price adds up operator kits by leaf count, the gate leaves themselves by opening width and material, new columns or posts when you are not reusing existing hardware, AC trenching or a solar kit, vehicle loops, a keypad, battery backup, extra remotes, edge sensors, a permit line, travel and equipment, overhead, and your target margin — all from the opening, style, and rates you enter, not a flat “automatic gate” price.

        Why does a dual swing cost more than a single swing on the same opening?

        A dual-swing gate is priced as two operators and typically three new columns against a single swing’s one operator and two columns, and its own starting hours and material rates run a little higher besides. The three-way comparison prices your same opening under single-swing, dual-swing, and slide starting kits so you can see which style actually wins once columns and operators are counted.

        Does the gate material change more than just the leaf price?

        Yes. Steel and wood carry a weight factor above aluminum, which raises both the leaf material cost and the hang hours for the same opening width, while vinyl and chain-link carry a weight factor below aluminum and lower both. Everything else — columns, power, loops, and access — prices the same regardless of leaf material.

        Is my data uploaded anywhere?

        No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage between visits, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page’s URL hash rather than sending anything to a server.

        What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

        The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — operators, leaves, columns, power, access hardware, and labor — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all.

        Does this check UL 325 safety requirements or electrical code?

        No. This is not a gate specification, a UL 325 determination, a permit, an electrical design, or an engineering stamp. Loops, keypads, battery backup, and edge sensors are line items you choose to include; whether a specific installation meets the safety standard is a judgment call for whoever pulls the permit, not something this arithmetic decides.

vs-a-flat-4500-special.html.text:
← Automatic driveway gate bid calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $4,500 special

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic pricing habit every gate shop competes with: one flat number — commonly a "$4,500 automatic gate" special — advertised the same regardless of opening width, material, columns, power, loops, or access.

First — the flat special is right, and you should have one

A Facebook ad or a yard sign needs a number before anyone has seen the driveway. "$4,500 installed" is a perfectly fine headline price, and no calculator replaces having one. What follows is not an argument that the flat number is wrong. It is what that same number stops showing you the moment an opening is real and you know its style, material, columns, power, and access.

The worked example

Both rows below are this calculator's own built-in starting jobs — the two ends of its catalogue — priced at its own shipped shop rates: a $42/hr crew wage, 32% burden, $285 travel and equipment, 16% overhead, a 28% target margin, and a $125 permit. The only thing that changes between them is the job.

QuestionCheap end — 12 ft single aluminum swing, existing posts, ACWhere the special loses — 16 ft dual steel swing, masonry, 2 loops, keypad, solar
What the flat special charges $4,500 — the gate $4,500 — the gate, unchanged
Operators / new columns 1 operator, 0 new columns (existing posts) 2 operators, 3 new masonry columns
Total crew hours 12.95 h 42.89 h — more than 3× the crew time
Material cost $3,035.00 $10,024.00 — masonry columns, two loops, keypad, and solar do not live in a per-opening special
Total cost before any profit $4,684.02 — already above the $4,500 flat special $14,716.71 — far above the $4,500 flat special
What the $4,500 flat special actually nets −$184.02 — a loss on the cheapest job in the catalogue −$10,216.71 — a loss more than double the flat price itself
This calculator's price at a 28% target margin $6,505.58 $20,439.88 — $13,934.30 more than the cheap-end price, for the same $4,500 headline
Effective crew rate the $4,500 flat special actually pays $347.49/hr (12.95 billed hours) $104.92/hr — a 70% cut from the cheap-end rate, at the identical advertised price

The two places the flat special goes quiet

1. Operators and columns never separate from the gate

A flat special answers "what do I charge for a gate," not "how many operators and columns this opening needs." Both live inside the same $4,500 either way. The calculator splits them out — 1 operator and 0 new columns on the cheap end, 2 operators and 3 masonry columns on the harder job — so the crew hours, the hardware, and the labor are visible numbers instead of one flat guess that happened to work out on a good day.

2. The same advertised price does not clear cost on either end

This is the one that costs real money. The flat special charges $4,500 whether the opening is the easiest job in the catalogue or the hardest, but the cost behind it is not the same — on this calculator's own defaults, even the cheap end already runs $184.02 over the flat price before a dollar of profit, and the harder job runs $10,216.71 over it. A shop quoting "the $4,500 special" on every call can sell every job on the price sheet and still lose money on each one, with nothing on the ad to say so.

When the flat special is still the better tool

For advertising, it plainly is. A yard sign or a Facebook ad cannot show a live calculator, and a homeowner calling for a price wants one number, not a form. The sensible arrangement is both: run the flat special to get the call, then run this calculator once you know the opening width, material, columns, power, loops, and access, to check whether that job's version of "the $4,500 gate" still covers the operators and the columns — and, on a job far enough from the cheap end, whether it needs a real bid instead.

Every figure on this page is this calculator's own worked example, computed from its own built-in starting jobs and shipped default shop rates, not a claim about any real shop's business or an industry benchmark. Your rates, wages, and overhead will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to produce, not what they should come out to.

Common questions

Is a flat $4,500 special wrong?

No, and it should not go away. A Facebook ad or a yard sign needs one number, and "$4,500 installed" is a fine headline price. The point of this page is not that the flat number is wrong — it is that the flat number is the same whether the opening is a 12-foot single aluminum swing on existing posts or a 16-foot dual steel swing on new masonry columns with loops and solar, and only a full bid separates the two.

Does the $4,500 special even cover the cheapest job in the catalogue?

On this calculator's own shipped defaults, no. The cheapest preset — a 12 ft single aluminum swing on existing posts with AC power — comes out to $4,684.02 in total cost before any profit is added, $184.02 above the flat $4,500 special. That is the easiest job the calculator prices, and the flat rate is already short of covering it.

How much worse does it get on a harder job?

A 16 ft dual steel swing on new masonry columns, with two vehicle loops, a keypad, and a solar kit, costs $14,716.71 on this calculator's own defaults — $10,216.71 more than the flat $4,500 special, before a dollar of profit. Two operators instead of one, three new masonry columns instead of zero, and the loop and solar hardware do not live inside a per-opening special.

Does the calculator replace the flat special?

No, and it is not trying to. The flat number is what you advertise to get the call. This calculator is what you run once you know the opening width, material, columns, power, loops, and access, to check whether that job's version of "the $4,500 gate" still covers the operators, the columns, and the crew hours — and, on a job far enough from the cheap end, whether it needs a real bid instead.

← Automatic Driveway Gate Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this automatic gate install cost, given its style, opening width, and power needs, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the gate style (single swing, dual swing, or slide), opening width, leaf material, whether new columns are needed, AC trenching versus a solar kit, vehicle loops, a keypad, battery backup, and extra remotes, plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money and where the bid's hours are actually going — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
